A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PieTa by the same authors. All nine pages of v3 and fourteen pages of v4, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, algorithms, figures, and tables.

before.justification: v3 reports original WikiSQL experiments measuring subtable precision/recall, downstream QA accuracy, and ablation results in Tables 1–7.

after.justification: v4 reports original WikiSQL and WikiTQ experiments, representation and window-size ablations, and additional TabSQLify sensitivity results. Appendix A.4 distinguishes reproduced comparisons from externally reported baseline results.

M1.justification: v3 generates selected tables containing headers, row indices, and cell values. v4 introduces coordinate-grid outputs with coordinate tokens for selected cells and empty tokens elsewhere (Section 3.3 and Figure A.1), substantially changing the selector’s output and training targets. The iterative divide, select, and union procedure remains.

E1.justification: v3 trains and evaluates on WikiSQL. v4 additionally evaluates WikiTQ and uses its SQUALL SQL annotations for training. This extends coverage to more compositional questions involving superlatives and comparisons, beyond the simpler WikiSQL questions (Section 4 and Appendix A.4).

E2.justification: The ITR, TabSQLify, and Holistic LM selection comparison remains. However, v4 substantially expands QA comparators: WikiSQL gains holistic TaPEx, CABINET, GPT-3.5, and StructGPT comparisons, while WikiTQ includes Dater, Binder, Chain-of-Table, ReAcTable, and DP&Agent (Tables 4–5). Appendix A.4 identifies which results were reproduced or taken from prior reports.

E3.justification: Reported selector settings change from Llama3-8B-Instruct, five epochs, and 3×3 windows to Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, one epoch, and default 4×4 windows. The in-context ablation changes from five shots to two. Ablations switch from selector precision/recall to TaPEx QA exact match on WikiSQL validation, and new GPT reader experiments introduce SQL/text answer-selection protocols.

E4.justification: v4 adds window-size sensitivity, coordinate-versus-table/index comparisons, and TabSQLify row-budget sensitivity (Table 6 and Appendix A.6). It removes v3’s balanced-versus-unbalanced performance ablation and table-size-binned selector precision/recall table. Iteration, answer-shape, and QA-versus-table-size analyses remain with revised or expanded evidence.

E5.justification: v4 Appendix A.4 newly specifies a single run per dataset and states that the algorithm has no random elements. v3 provides no corresponding run information. Neither reports confidence intervals or significance tests; the new disclosure does not establish a reduction in runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces PieTa’s reported precision/recall of 51.2/97.8 with 60.88/99.12 and TabSQLify’s 13.7/80.5 with 75.47/87.36. WikiSQL OmniTab-plus-PieTa EM changes from 88.55 to 91.17, and reported TabSQLify SQL failures change from 10,691 to 425. Numerous WikiTQ and ablation results are added. These are revised results under changed configurations, not controlled same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The admissible target-size enumeration changes from w(w+1)+1, including 0×0 in v3 Section 3.2, to w(w+1), explicitly excluding [0,0] in v4 Appendix A.5. This is a limited revision to a mathematical definition/count. No theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: Both abstracts, introductions, and conclusions retain the central claim that iterative window selection and union capture dependencies while mitigating long-context difficulties and improving subtable-based QA. Naming WikiTQ adds supporting evaluation scope without materially redefining that overarching claim.

C2.justification: v3 explains the benefit of table-valued outputs over indices. v4 substantially extends this account with limitations of both representations, autoregressive error propagation, and the proposed coordinate mechanism (Section 3.3). It also interprets new sensitivity results, acknowledges the TabSQLify–TaPEx exception on WikiTQ, and discusses selective-sampling and adversarial risks. The reader–selector joint-optimization limitation remains.

D1.justification: v4 adds hardware, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, gradient accumulation, training time, GPT reader prompts and execution rules, target-label augmentation details, and baseline-result provenance (Appendices A.3–A.4). It promises code release upon acceptance without establishing current availability. Conversely, v3’s explicit 56,355 training-pair count and output-layer-only tuning specification disappear.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations supporting autoregressive-error explanations, SQUALL supervision, additional QA baselines, and SQL-generation failures. These are localized extensions; the main positioning against holistic readers, ITR, Dater, and TabSQLify remains. The updated publication details for Rethinking Tabular Data Understanding refer to an already cited work.

P1.justification: Prose is extensively revised across the abstract, introduction, related work, methods, and results. Training-window sampling moves principally into Appendix A.5, experimental details move into expanded appendices, selection and QA results receive separate subsections, and references precede the appendix. Terminology and selector notation are also clarified.

P2.justification: v4 redraws the overview and training examples, adds the representation illustration and GPT prompt figure, and substantially restructures comparison tables. QA-by-size results become two benchmark plots, while training histograms receive new arrangements and axes. Document typography, spacing, and figure placement change throughout; the earlier union-table example is retained as Figure 4.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of the claimed reader-independent framework: v3’s main QA comparison is limited to WikiSQL with OmniTab, whereas v4 tests compositional WikiTQ questions and multiple specialist and generalist readers. Representation/window ablations and explicit baseline configurations and provenance further improve assessability. The lost balancing ablation and some omitted training details are drawbacks, and uncertainty remains unquantified, but the broader, better documented validation provides a substantial net improvement.
